explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Isaiah flips it. He says, "Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear." So the LORD's reach is just fine. It's an easy one to turn around when you're reading fast. I've misread a recipe the same way and ended up with a very sad batch.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says the LORD's arm is "not too short to save," and His ear isn't too dull to hear either. So whatever has gone quiet, it isn't because He can't reach or can't listen. Hold onto that. The rest of the passage depends on it.

Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God." He adds that their sins have hidden His face from them. Picture a wall the people stacked up themselves, brick by brick, with nobody else holding the trowel.

Armies do sound like a solid suspect, I'll give you that. But Isaiah never mentions one here. He says the barriers come from the people's own iniquities, and that their sins have hidden His face from them.

Altars are a fair guess, baker, since they're such a big part of worship. But nothing in these verses says a word about altars. Isaiah points at the people's own iniquities as the thing that built the barriers.
That's it, friend. Isaiah says, "your lips have spoken lies, and your tongue mutters injustice." Right alongside the stained hands, the mouth is in on it too. Hands and lips both get called out.
Curses would be a rough way to talk, but that's not the word Isaiah uses. He says their lips have spoken lies, and that their tongue mutters injustice. Same mouth, different problem.
Boasting is a real thing people do, baker, but Isaiah doesn't name it here. What he says is, "your lips have spoken lies." I'd pick that one next time.
Right, baker. Isaiah says, "No one calls for justice; no one pleads his case honestly." Not a single honest voice in the room. That's a heavy line, and he says it plainly.

That's the exact opposite, friend. Isaiah says, "No one calls for justice; no one pleads his case honestly." Nobody is doing it honestly, not even a few. It's easy to flip when the blank is only one word.
Isaiah doesn't single out any group here, baker. He says, "No one calls for justice; no one pleads his case honestly." So the blank is "no one," with nobody left out.
Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "Whoever eats their eggs will die." And if you crack one open, "a viper is hatched." I don't know about you, but I'm checking every carton from now on.
Feeling sick sounds bad enough, baker, but Isaiah goes further. He says, "Whoever eats their eggs will die." No sick day, no recovery. That's how serious the picture is.
A nap would be a gentle ending, friend, and Isaiah isn't gentle here. He says, "Whoever eats their eggs will die." These are viper eggs, so this is not a cozy moment.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says, "Their cobwebs cannot be made into clothing, and they cannot cover themselves with their works." I've worn an apron through a lot of flour storms, and I promise it was never made of cobweb. Their works can't cover them either.
Rope would at least be useful, friend. But Isaiah says the cobwebs "cannot be made into clothing." The point is that their works can't cover them.
Sails are a creative guess, baker, and I like the imagination. But Isaiah doesn't mention boats anywhere in these verses. He says the cobwebs "cannot be made into clothing."
True, friend. Isaiah says, "Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood." Notice the word run. They're not wandering toward it or stumbling into it.
Not this time, baker. Isaiah says, "Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood." So the feet are running toward evil. It's a hard line, but that's what the text says.
Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "no one who treads on them will know peace." He'd already said that "The way of peace they have not known." Crooked paths don't lead there.
Wealth is a natural guess, baker, since people chase it down all kinds of roads. But Isaiah says, "no one who treads on them will know peace." Peace is the word that fits the blank.
Honor sounds like it belongs on a list like that, friend. But Isaiah doesn't use it here. He says, "no one who treads on them will know peace."
That's it, baker. The voice says, "justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us." It's a heavy thing to say out loud. I think that's why the switch to "us" lands so hard.
Enemies don't come up in this verse, friend. The "we" voice says, "justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us." Justice is what's far away.
Homeland is an understandable guess, baker. But this verse never says it's far away. It says, "justice is far from us."

Right, friend. The voice says, "Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall, groping like those without eyes." You know that late-night walk to the kitchen with the lights off? Hand on the wall, praying you miss the furniture. It's that, only far more serious.
Lost fits the feeling, baker, but it isn't the word in the verse. It says, "Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall." The picture is of people who can't see.
Weary is a believable pick, friend. But the verse says, "Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall." It's about not being able to see, more than about being tired.
Not quite, baker. The voice says, "We stumble at midday as in the twilight." Midday is the brightest part of the day. So the stumbling isn't just for nighttime.
Yes, friend. The voice says, "We stumble at midday as in the twilight." Even in full daylight, they're tripping like it's dusk. That tells you how deep the gloom is.
Not here, baker. The voice says they hope "for salvation, but it is far from us." So it isn't close at hand. That's why the groping and the groaning sound so heavy.

That's right, friend. The voice says, "We hope for justice, but find none, for salvation, but it is far from us." They're hoping, and it hasn't arrived. Keep that in mind, because this isn't where it ends.
Yes, baker. The voice says, "our sins testify against us." Nobody else had to be called to the stand. Their own sins do the talking.
Neighbors would make for a nosy courtroom, friend. But the voice says, "our sins testify against us." The witness is their own sins.
The prophets are a natural guess, baker, since they did speak for God. But here the voice says, "our sins testify against us." The sins themselves are the witness.
True, baker. The voice says, "Our transgressions are indeed with us, and we know our iniquities." They're not pretending or hiding. That honest moment matters.
Actually the opposite, friend. The voice says, "we know our iniquities." They aren't claiming surprise. They're owning it, and that's a big step.
That's it, friend. The voice confesses "conceiving and uttering lies from the heart." So the lies don't just come out of the mouth. They start deeper in.
A crowd can pile on, baker, I'll give you that. But the verse says "conceiving and uttering lies from the heart." The confession is about the heart, where it starts.
The past is a reasonable guess, friend. But the verse says, "conceiving and uttering lies from the heart." That's where it starts, according to the voice.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "truth has stumbled in the public square." That's the open place where everybody gathers. If truth is tripping there, everyone can see it.
Temple courts are a fair guess, friend, but they're not named here. The verse says, "truth has stumbled in the public square." So it's out in the open, where everybody can see it.
A palace would make a dramatic spot, baker. But the verse doesn't mention the king or a palace. It says, "truth has stumbled in the public square."
Not quite, friend. The verse says, "honesty cannot enter." So honesty isn't walking right in. It's being kept out.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says truth stumbled, and "honesty cannot enter." The door is shut on it. And a sad scene like that is exactly what sets up what the LORD does next.
Right, friend. Isaiah says, "The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice." He saw it, and it displeased Him. That's the reason the next verses move the way they do.
An empty temple does sound like something that would bother Him, baker. But the verse doesn't say that. It says, "The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice."
Fasting did come up earlier in the book, friend, but not in this verse. Here Isaiah says, "The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice." Justice is what He found missing.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "So His own arm brought salvation." And remember how the passage began, with the arm that isn't too short to save? Here it is, doing the saving.
His word is powerful, friend, but it isn't what this verse names. Isaiah says, "So His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him." The arm is the answer.
A sign sounds dramatic, baker, but the verse doesn't mention one. It says, "So His own arm brought salvation." The arm is what stepped in.
That's it, friend. Isaiah says He "wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal." Breastplate, helmet, garments, and now a cloak. That's the full outfit.
A robe of peace sounds comfortable, baker, but it isn't in the verse. Isaiah says He "wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal." Zeal is the word here.
Mourning clothes are a believable guess, friend. But the verse says He "wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal." That's the piece of clothing Isaiah names.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "So He will repay according to their deeds." It's about what people actually did. The word is deeds.
Wealth is a common measuring stick, friend, but Isaiah doesn't use it here. He says, "So He will repay according to their deeds." Deeds is the answer.
Prayers is a thoughtful guess, baker, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "So He will repay according to their deeds." What people did is the measure.
True, friend. Isaiah says, "So shall they fear the name of the LORD where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises." West and east, both named. His name reaches all the way around.
Not this time, baker. Isaiah says, "So shall they fear the name of the LORD where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises." So the sunset side is included, and so is the sunrise side.
True, baker. Isaiah says, "For He will come like a raging flood, driven by the breath of the LORD." The breath of the LORD is what drives it. That's a lot of force.
Not quite, friend. Isaiah says the flood is "driven by the breath of the LORD." So that is exactly what's behind it.
Yes, friend. The LORD declares, "The Redeemer will come to Zion." After all that darkness, that's good news. Salvation was far away, and now here comes Someone to bring it near.
Avenger fits the vengeance garments from earlier, baker. But in this verse the LORD says, "The Redeemer will come to Zion." Redeemer is the word He uses.
Conqueror sounds like it would go with the armor, friend. But the LORD declares, "The Redeemer will come to Zion." So the word is Redeemer.
That's right, baker. The LORD says the Redeemer comes "to those in Jacob who turn from transgression." The door is open to those who turn. Jacob here means the people of Israel.

explanations.answer: Those who bring the most offerings
explanations.explanation: Offerings are a typical guess, friend, but the verse never mentions them. The LORD says the Redeemer comes "to those in Jacob who turn from transgression." Turning is what He names.
Winning is a very human way to measure people, baker. But the LORD says the Redeemer comes "to those in Jacob who turn from transgression." Turning from transgression is what He names.
Yes, friend. The LORD says, "My Spirit will not depart from you." That's a promise. And it comes with His words staying in their mouths too.
The temple is a big part of the story, baker, but it isn't what He names here. The LORD says, "My Spirit will not depart from you." His Spirit is the answer.
Prophets did a lot of speaking for Him, friend, but they're not in this promise. The LORD says, "My Spirit will not depart from you." It's His Spirit.

Not quite, baker. The LORD says His words will not depart "from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore." That reaches well past one generation. It's the opposite of a one-time hand-off.

That's right, friend. The LORD says His words will not depart from your mouth "or from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore." Children, then grandchildren, then onward. It's a promise with no end date.
